newsitem.title: USA: Hashimoto promises more cooperation with U.S.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto promises more cooperation with U.S.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto wrapped up a visit to Washington on Saturday that confirmed expanded bilateral cooperation with the United States in forging economic and security ties.

In a meeting on Saturday with Vice President Al Gore, Hashimoto agreed that Japan and the United States would increase cooperation on global issues such as protection of the environment, the fight against acid rain in Asia and the warming of the Earth, and support for democratization of developing countries, Japanese officials said.

During his 48 hours in Washington, part of a tour that will also take him to Australia and New Zealand, he held a three-hour official meeting with President Bill Clinton that focused on Japan's huge trade surplus with the United States and the U.S. military presence in Japan.

Hashimoto assured Clinton that Japan was not asking for a cut in American military forces in Japan and Asia. Hashimoto's plane left Andrews Air Force Base near Washington at 5:50 p.m. EDT (2150 GMT) to head to Honolulu, according to a U.S. military spokesman.
The governor of Okinawa, where Japanese object to a continued large-scale U.S. presence, is urging Hashimoto to call on Washington to cut back its military presence.

The governor, Masahide Ota, also opposed the enactment last week of a key bill to extend leases on land for U.S. military bases on the island, enabling the central government to override local opposition to the contracts.
Clinton applauded Hashimoto's efforts to pass the bill through parliament, which Hashimoto said was necessary for Japan to respect the Japan-U.S. security treaty, Japanese officials said.

In a brief meeting with Defence Secretary William Cohen on Saturday, Hashimoto assured the U.S. that it completes an update of Japan-U.S. 1978 joint "defense guidelines" for security cooperation by autumn this year.
The U.S. wanted assurances that U.S. forces could use bases in Japan for operations or transportation in case of a new war in Korea.
U.S. officials have said Japanese forces also might help evacuate civilians threatened by such a conflict.

A senior Japanese government official told reporters that Japan will make sure neighbouring Asian countries like China will not have a wrong impression that the guidelines will lead to Japan's military expansion.
On economic issues, Hashimoto and Clinton agreed Japan should avoid a substantial rise in its trade surplus with the U.S. and promote strong domestic demand-led economic growth.

"Structural changes in Japan have had positive impact on bilateral economic relations and Japanese trade surplus with the U.S. is diminishing as a long-term trend," Hashimoto said in a speech to the National Press Club Friday.
Washington has repeatedly called on Japan not to depend on stepped-up exports to fuel faster growth and instead to enliven domestic demand so as to absorb more imports.
Japan's surplus with the U.S. has been rising over the past six months from year-earlier levels. It rose to $3.04 billion in March, up 11.2 percent from March 1996.
